title: Lumenary Robotics
subtitle: Robotics from a first moving robot to the learning-based humanoids of 2026: motion, control, perception, planning, real robot systems, robot learning and the frontier.
description: Lumenary Robotics is the fourth subject of Lumenary Scientia, free and open source like the others. It starts with no experience at all — what makes a machine a robot — and climbs through the mathematics of motion, control, perception and state estimation, and planning, to how real robots are built and how robots learn, ending with the vision-language-action models and humanoids that research labs and companies are building in 2026.

Every lesson teaches with ideas first and code second. Robots are simulated in Python with NumPy, and every block with a **Run in browser** button runs there, with nothing to install: you will drive simulated robots, fuse noisy sensors, plan paths and train small policies yourself. A lesson says *Code tested* only when all of its code passed. Lumenary Robotics builds on [Lumenary CS](/en/cs/) for programming, algorithms and machine learning, and on [Lumenary EE](/en/ee/) for circuits, motors and control.
Real robots can hurt people. Lessons that touch hardware say what is safe to try — small, slow, battery-powered robots — and why industrial machines are fenced, rated and certified.

Every lesson was drafted with AI assistance and is awaiting review by a human roboticist. The text, exercises and code are original and licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 (code Apache-2.0). Where a lab, company or project has published the primary source — a paper, a dataset, a design document — the lesson links to it rather than retelling it.

levels.title: What robots are
levels.summary: No experience needed, from about age 11. What makes a machine a robot, how robots sense the world and move in it, your first robot program in a simulated world, and how robots and people work safely together.

levels.title: The mathematics of motion
levels.summary: Describing where things are and how they move: frames and rigid transforms, rotations and quaternions, wheeled robots and odometry, forward and inverse kinematics of arms, Jacobians, and dynamics.

levels.title: Control
levels.summary: Making a robot do what we mean: feedback and PID, state-space models, LQR and observers, trajectories and tracking, force and impedance control, and model predictive control.

levels.title: Perception and state estimation
levels.summary: Knowing the world under uncertainty: Bayes filters, Kalman filters, particle filters and localisation, cameras and computer vision, depth sensing and point clouds, and simultaneous localisation and mapping.

levels.title: Planning and decision-making
levels.summary: Deciding where to go and what to do: search on graphs and grids, sampling-based planners, configuration spaces and collision checking, trajectory optimisation, and task planning with behaviour trees.

levels.title: Building real robots
levels.summary: From parts to working machines: ROS 2 and robot software, simulation, embedded control and functional safety, manipulation and grasping, legged robots, aerial robots, autonomous vehicles, and teams of robots.

levels.title: Robot learning
levels.summary: Robots that learn from experience and from demonstration: reinforcement learning for control, imitation learning, crossing the gap between simulation and reality, and the large datasets behind today's generalist policies.

levels.title: The frontier of robotics
levels.summary: Where robotics stands in 2026, with links to the labs' own papers: vision-language-action models, humanoid robots, world models, dexterous hands and touch, and how learned robots are evaluated and deployed safely.
